extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; citizens, lawmakers, and scholars interested in legitimacy, resistance, and dissolution of government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for when a government is dissolved or forfeits legitimacy, when people may erect a new legislative or resist authority, and who may judge such questions. Includes limits on lawful resistance and examples of acts that cause forfeiture of governmental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of legislative powers dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When these are taken away or altered, so as to deprive the society of the due exercise of their power, the legislative is truly altered; for it is not names that constitute governments, but the use and exercise of those powers that were intended to accompany them;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on removal or alteration of the use/exercise of legislative powers (not merely titles). If the legislature's functional powers are deprived, the legislative is 'truly altered' and government is dissolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering electors or the ways of election dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by the arbitrary power of the prince, the electors, or ways of election, are altered, without the consent, and contrary to the common interest of the people, there also the legislative is altered:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing who chooses representatives or the method of election without consent and against the common interest produces an altered legislative and undermines the legitimacy of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of the people into subjection to a foreign power dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery also of the people into the subjection of a foreign power, either by the prince, or by the legislative, is certainly a change of the legislative, and so a dissolution of the government:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rulers transfer the people under foreign dominion, the social end (preservation as an independent society) is lost and the government is dissolved; loss of national independence counts as forfeiture of legitimate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect or abandonment of executive that prevents execution of laws dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When he who has the supreme executive power, neglects and abandons that charge, so that the laws already made can no longer be put in execution. This is demonstratively to reduce all to anarchy, and so effectually to dissolve the government:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government's existence depends on the administration and enforcement of law; if the executive fails so laws cannot be executed and there is no power to direct force or secure rights, there is effectively no government.

rubrics_metrics.name: People have a right to erect a new legislative when government is dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves, by erecting a new legislative, differing from the other, by the change of persons, or form, or both, as they shall find it most for their safety and good:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The society retains its original right to preserve itself; if the existing legislative has been removed or destroyed by oppression/artifice/foreign power, the people may establish a new legislative to secure safety and the ends of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative acts against the trust (invading property) forfeit authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative acts against the trust reposed in them, when they endeavour to invade the property of the subject, and to make themselves, or any part of the community, masters, or arbitrary disposers of the lives, liberties, or fortunes of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If legislators attempt to destroy or take away people's property or reduce them to slavery—i.e., act contrary to the end of government—they forfeit the power entrusted to them and place themselves in a state of war with the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive/prince acts against trust by setting up arbitrary will or corrupting representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: He, who having a double trust... acts against both, when he goes about to set up his own arbitrary will as the law of the society. He acts also contrary to his trust, when he either employs the force, treasure, and offices of the society, to corrupt the representatives, and gain them to his purposes; or openly preengages the electors, and prescribes to their choice...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive action that subverts representative choice—through corruption, preengaging electors, controlling candidates—or seeks to impose arbitrary will, is a breach of trust and grounds for resistance or reconstitution of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of power results in people's right to resume original liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the legislators endeavour to take away, and destroy the property of the people, or to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are thereupon absolved from any farther obedience...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When governing bodies betray their trust by aiming at arbitrary dominion over life, liberty, or property, authority reverts to the people who may resume their liberty and establish a new legislative suited to their safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions justified only after long train of abuses making designs visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Such revolutions happen not upon every little mismanagement in public affairs... But if a long train of abuses, prevarications and artifices, all tending the same way, make the design visible to the people... it is not to be wondered, that they should then rouse themselves...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor mistakes do not justify revolution; legitimate resistance or regime change requires a clear, sustained pattern of abuse or a visible design against the people's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to erect new legislative is the best guard against rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: This doctrine of a power in the people of providing for their safety a-new, by a new legislative, when their legislators have acted contrary to their trust... is the best fence against rebellion, and the probablest means to hinder it:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing a lawful remedy—reestablishing legislative authority—channels resistance away from arbitrary rebellion and helps distinguish legitimate defense of rights from unlawful insurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who change legislative or act contrary to trust are rebels
rubrics_metrics.description: In both the fore-mentioned cases, when either the legislative is changed, or the legislators act contrary to the end for which they were constituted; those who are guilty are guilty of rebellion: for if any one by force takes away the established legislative... they actually introduce a state of war...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both usurpers who remove legislatures by force and legislators who put themselves into a state of war with the people by invading rights are to be considered rebels (i.e., guilty of the greatest crime against commonwealth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance allowed against magistrates who use force without right; self-defence extends to the community
rubrics_metrics.description: That subjects or foreigners, attempting by force on the properties of any people, may be resisted with force, is agreed on all hands. But that magistrates, doing the same thing, may be resisted, hath of late been denied... Self-defence is a part of the law of nature; nor can it be denied the community, even against the king himself:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force used without legal right places the aggressor in a state of war and cancels former ties; the community has a right of self-defense against unjust magistrates as well as against external aggressors, subject to limits below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on resistance: defense not revenge; must not punish superior beyond defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-defence is... allowed the community... but to revenge themselves upon him, must by no means be allowed them; it being not agreeable to that law. Wherefore... the people have a right to resist and defend themselves from injury: but it must be with this caution, that they only defend themselves, but do not attack their prince: they may repair the damages received, but must not for any provocation exceed the bounds of due reverence and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance should be corrective/defensive and not an act of retribution or humiliation of a superior; it should repel present attacks and prevent future mischief rather than enact vengeance for past wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of restrictions 'with reverence' and 'without retribution' on resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: He has annexed two limitations to it, to no purpose: First, He says, it must be with reverence. Secondly, It must be without retribution, or punishment... How to resist force without striking again, or how to strike with reverence, will need some skill to make intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical limits requiring resistance to be 'with reverence' and 'without punishment' are incoherent; effective resistance necessarily may include striking and, in the state of war, the victor has a right to punish the aggressor for breach of the peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two cases where a king ceases to be king and may be resisted
rubrics_metrics.description: Two cases there are... whereby a king, ipso facto, becomes no king, and loses all power and regal authority over his people: (1) If he endeavour to overturn the government... (2) If he makes himself the dependent of another, and subjects his kingdom... to the dominion of another:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Nero, Caligula) illustrate the first case (actively seeking to ruin kingdom). The second case is alienation of the kingdom to foreign power. In either case the king forfeits regal authority and the people may treat him as a private person.

rubrics_metrics.name: The people shall be judge whether prince or legislative act contrary to trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Who shall be judge, whether the prince or legislative act contrary to their trust? ... The people shall be judge; for who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well, and according to the trust reposed in him, but he who deputes him...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In matters where legislative or executive conduct goes beyond trust, the proper umpire is the body of the people. In disputes where law is silent or doubtful and of great consequence, appeal to the people is appropriate; if no earthly judge exists, appeal lies to God and each person judges for himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where law is silent/doubtful and no superior exists, appeal to heaven/individual judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prince, or whoever they be in the administration, decline that way of determination, the appeal then lies no where but to heaven; force between either persons, who have no known superior on earth, or which permits no appeal to a judge on earth, being properly a state of war, wherein the appeal lies only to heaven; and in that state the injured party must judge for himself...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When no earthly arbiter can resolve a grave controversy about rights vs. authority, individuals or the people may judge and act, recognizing a final appeal to God; such situations characterize a state of war between rulers and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power given to society does not revert to individuals while society endures
rubrics_metrics.description: The power that every individual gave the society, when he entered into it, can never revert to the individuals again, as long as the society lasts, but will always remain in the community; ... when the society hath placed the legislative in any assembly of men, to continue in them and their successors... the legislative can never revert to the people whilst that government lasts;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once political power is vested in a community and a legislative instituted to continue, individuals do not individually resume that power while the society endures; authority remains communal and institutional until the government is dissolved by the conditions described above.
